summary:
Djibouti has no statute that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Articles 353 and 354 of the penal code refer vaguely to "good morals" and public morality without naming same-sex relations, and no provision states the position either way. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, nevertheless marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country in its at-a-glance assessment, and authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these articles. The practical position is that such conduct is treated as de facto illegal despite the absence of an express offence.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people. No reported case law defines the outer limits of Articles 353 and 354, so the exposure of a trans visitor who is visible, or who engages in any same-sex conduct in a public setting, cannot be predicted from the text.

Legal gender recognition is not available. LGBTI organisations cannot register. Discrimination protection exists in employment only; there is no broader legal prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity.

Status and conduct are treated as taboo. The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report describes a societal pattern of discrimination with no official violence cases citable, and pervasive social and religious intolerance that makes people fear family and community shunning on disclosure. No public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.

Complaints can be filed with police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH), though the report cites no cases of official violence.
tangentialFactors:
Djibouti's legal framework offers no hate-crime enhancement for bias-motivated violence, and no source in the inventory documents a specific trans-related violent incident with date or outcome.

The 2015 US State Department report for Djibouti contains limited LGBT-specific content; the remainder of that report addresses general conditions including suppression of the opposition, harsh prison conditions, FGM and trafficking, none of which bear directly on a trans visitor's legal exposure.

Compared with jurisdictions that maintain explicit criminalising statutes, Djibouti's exposure rests on vague morality provisions rather than a named offence, which makes the boundary of enforcement less predictable rather than more permissive.
localsOnly:
Djibouti's residents can seek redress for discrimination through employment-law channels, the only area where discrimination protection is reported to exist, and through complaints to police or the national human-rights commission (CNDH).

LGBTI organisations cannot register as legal entities, limiting organised advocacy and support services available to residents.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so residents have no formal mechanism to align official documents with lived gender.

Disclosure carries substantial social risk: pervasive social and religious intolerance means residents fear family and community shunning, and no public societal discussion of homosexuality is tolerated.
outOfScopeNotes:
No reported case law defines the outer limits of Articles 353 and 354 of the penal code; the boundary between lawful private conduct and prosecutable "obscene acts" or public-morality offences is unresolved in the sourced material.

No source in the inventory documents a specific trans-related violent incident in Djibouti with a date, perpetrator and outcome; the 2023 US State Department report cites no official violence cases.

Whether a trans visitor's documents or presentation would trigger additional scrutiny at entry, and how Djibouti's border and immigration authorities handle gender markers, is not sourced in the inventory.

Canadian IRB research from 2009 to March 2012 (response DJI104070.E) found documentation on treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti to be scarce across all consulted sources, leaning on the US 2010 country report; that historical baseline indicates how little legal, protection and support framework existed at the time, but its currency for present-day conditions is unresolved.
